questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify the atom that names a functional group
questions.stem: A student is asked which atom in a compound identifies the group as an amine. Which choice names that atom correctly?

options.text: The nitrogen atom bonded to one, two, or three carbon atoms
The carbon atom that is attached to the nitrogen by a single bond
options.misconception: believes the naming atom is the neighbouring carbon rather than the nitrogen

options.text: The oxygen atom of any water molecule trapped beside the group
options.misconception: believes water is the atom that defines an amine group

options.text: The hydrogen atom bonded to the nitrogen of the functional group
options.misconception: believes a hydrogen on nitrogen is what makes a compound an amine

questions.explanation: A functional group is named for the atom at its heart, and for an amine that atom is nitrogen: primary, secondary and tertiary amines differ only in how many carbons are attached to that nitrogen. The neighbouring carbon belongs to the rest of the chain, and a hydrogen on nitrogen is a feature of primary and secondary amines rather than the identifying feature, so naming either of those would mislabel the group.
questions.hint: Ask which atom of the group is different from the atoms in the carbon chain.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: deduce the hybridisation of arene ring carbons
questions.stem: Every carbon of a benzene ring carries one hydrogen and two ring bonds. What does that arrangement say about the ring?

options.text: The carbons are sp2 hybridised and planar, each with one unhybridised p orbital
The carbons are sp3 hybridised and tetrahedral, each with two p orbitals left over
options.misconception: believes four sigma bonds force sp3 and invents a second free p orbital

options.text: The carbons are sp hybridised and linear, each with two unhybridised p orbitals
options.misconception: believes a ring carbon with three sigma bonds is sp hybridised like a triple bond

options.text: The carbons are sp2 hybridised, but the ring puckers into a chair to relieve strain
options.misconception: believes sp2 carbons must pucker, which is a cyclohexane property

questions.explanation: Each ring carbon forms three sigma bonds, two to ring neighbours and one to hydrogen, so it uses sp2 hybridisation with the three hybrid orbitals in one plane and one unhybridised p orbital standing above that plane. Those parallel p orbitals overlap around the ring and hold it planar, which is also why a six-membered sp2 ring is flat while a sp3 ring puckers into a chair.
questions.hint: Count the sigma bonds on one ring carbon before choosing a hybridisation.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state what varies along a homologous series
questions.stem: Two consecutive members of an alkane homologous series are written out. What single change separates every member from the one before it?

options.text: One extra carbon together with two extra hydrogens, a CH2 unit
One extra carbon together with two extra oxygens, a CO2 unit
options.misconception: believes the repeating step in an alkane series brings in oxygen

options.text: One extra hydrogen together with one extra carbon, a CH unit
options.misconception: believes the step is a CH unit, which is a ring closure rather than a series step

options.text: One extra oxygen together with two extra hydrogens, an H2O unit
options.misconception: believes the alkane series repeats water, which belongs to no hydrocarbon series

questions.explanation: An alkane series runs C1H4, C2H6, C3H8 and so on, so each step adds one carbon and two hydrogens. Because the repeating unit is CH2 with a mass of 14.03 g per mol, consecutive members differ in molar mass by that fixed amount while their functional character, all single bonds and no functional group at all, stays the same.
questions.hint: Write the first three alkane formulas and look at the difference.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish constitutional isomers from stereoisomers
questions.stem: Two compounds share the molecular formula C4H10, one drawn as a straight chain and one drawn with a branch. How should the pair be classified?

options.text: Constitutional isomers, because the atoms of the same elements are connected differently
Stereoisomers, because the atoms of the same elements are connected identically
options.misconception: believes a change of shape alone makes a pair stereoisomers

options.text: Enantiomers, because one drawing is the mirror image of the other
options.misconception: believes a branched chain is the mirror image of a straight chain

options.text: Diastereomers, because the two drawings are non-superimposable mirror images
options.misconception: labels a connectivity difference as a mirror-image relationship

questions.explanation: Isomers share a formula, and the class depends on what is held constant. A constitutional pair holds the bonding pattern different, so butane and 2-methylpropane are constitutional isomers with different boiling points. A stereoisomer pair holds the connectivity identical and differs only in spatial arrangement, which cannot be said of a straight chain against a branched one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two drawings can be converted one into the other by bending bonds only.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Requirements for cis and trans isomerism
questions.learningObjective: state the structural requirement for geometric isomerism
questions.stem: When can two groups be placed on the same side or on opposite sides of a double bond in a genuine pair of geometric isomers?

options.text: When rotation about the double bond is blocked and each end carbon carries two different groups
When the double bond rotates freely and each end carbon carries two identical groups
options.misconception: believes free rotation and identical groups still produce a defined pair

options.text: When the ring is large enough that single bonds inside it can rotate freely
options.misconception: believes ring size and single bond rotation govern double bond geometry

options.text: When each end carbon carries the same group on both of its positions
options.misconception: believes matching groups on each carbon still allow a cis or trans pair

questions.explanation: Geometric isomerism needs two conditions at once. Rotation must be blocked, and it is blocked by the pi part of a double bond or by the ring in a cycloalkane, so the two arrangements cannot interconvert. Each doubly bonded atom must also carry two different groups, because if one carbon carries two hydrogens there is only one arrangement and cis or trans is not defined at all.
questions.hint: Two conditions are needed: a rigid framework and different groups on each end.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state what a chiral centre produces
questions.stem: One carbon of a molecule carries four different groups, so that molecule is chiral. What necessarily follows?

options.text: A non-superimposable mirror image exists, and the two forms rotate polarised light equally but oppositely
The mirror image is superimposable, so the molecule shows no optical activity at all
options.misconception: believes a chiral centre still allows the mirror image to coincide

options.text: The molecule is achiral, because four different groups cancel one another's effects
options.misconception: believes four different substituents neutralise each other

options.text: Only one stereoisomer can exist, because the four groups are held in a fixed arrangement
options.misconception: believes a fixed arrangement means only one form is possible

questions.explanation: A carbon with four different groups has no internal mirror plane, so the mirror image cannot be rotated back onto the original and the two forms are a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers share every bulk property except the direction of rotation of plane polarised light, which is why the pair is hard to tell apart and needs polarimetry to separate.
questions.hint: Ask whether the mirror image can be superimposed on the original drawing.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: predict the optical behaviour of a racemic mixture
questions.stem: A synthesis produces equal amounts of the two enantiomers of a chiral compound. What does the resulting mixture do to plane polarised light?

options.text: Nothing net, because the equal and opposite rotations of the two enantiomers cancel
It rotates the light, because both enantiomers rotate it in the same direction
options.misconception: believes mirror-image forms must rotate light the same way

options.text: It rotates the light twice as far as either pure enantiomer would on its own
options.misconception: believes combining two optically active samples doubles the rotation

options.text: It does nothing because each enantiomer is individually achiral
options.misconception: believes an optically active enantiomer can be achiral

questions.explanation: A 50 to 50 mixture of enantiomers is called racemic, and the two rotations are equal in size and opposite in sign because the two structures are mirror images. The observed rotation of the mixture is the sum of the contributions, so it is zero, and the mixture is optically inactive even though the molecules inside it are not.
questions.hint: Add the two rotations as signed quantities, not as magnitudes.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: assign nucleophile and electrophile in a reaction
questions.stem: A bromide ion is about to react with the carbon of a methyl group. Which statement assigns the two roles in that step correctly?

options.text: The bromide ion is the nucleophile and the methyl carbon is the electrophile
The bromide ion is the electrophile and the methyl carbon is the nucleophile
options.misconception: swaps the electron donor and the electron acceptor

options.text: Both are nucleophiles, because both carry the same charge at that carbon
options.misconception: believes sharing a charge makes both partners donors

options.text: Both are electrophiles, because both are drawn towards the bromide charge
options.misconception: believes attraction to an anion makes both partners acceptors

questions.explanation: A nucleophile donates a lone pair, and a bromide ion carries filled non-bonding pairs, so it is the electron-rich partner. An electrophile accepts a pair, and the carbon of a methyl group bonded to a good leaving group is electron-poor, so it is the electron-poor partner. Electron density always flows from the nucleophile to the electrophile.
questions.hint: Ask which partner has lone pairs to give and which needs electrons.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Substrate preference for a one-step substitution
questions.learningObjective: predict the substrate a one-step substitution favours
questions.stem: A substitution reaction is run by the single-step pathway rather than the stepwise one. Which substrate does that pathway serve best?

options.text: A methyl or primary halide, where the electrophilic carbon is least crowded
A tertiary halide, where the electrophilic carbon is most crowded
options.misconception: believes the most crowded carbon is easiest for a concerted attack

options.text: Any halide equally well, because crowding never matters in a one-step path
options.misconception: believes steric effects disappear in a concerted mechanism

options.text: A vinyl halide, because the double bond makes the carbon especially open
options.misconception: believes a double bond loosens the carbon for a concerted backside attack

questions.explanation: The one-step path needs the nucleophile to reach the carbon and the carbon to reach a partly broken bond at the same time, so it is a backside approach that suffers badly from steric crowding. Methyl and primary carbons are the least crowded and react fastest this way, while tertiary carbons are so blocked that they fall back on the two-step path instead. A vinyl carbon is worse still, because the partial positive charge of a vinyl halide sits on an sp2 carbon held tightly by the extra bond.
questions.hint: Think about the approach angle a nucleophile needs to the reaction centre.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish E1 from E2 elimination
questions.stem: Two elimination pathways compete for the same substrate. Which comparison of E1 and E2 is correct?

options.text: E2 is one step and needs a strong base, while E1 ionises first and works with a weak base
E1 is one step and needs a strong base, while E2 ionises first and works with a weak base
options.misconception: swaps which pathway is concerted and which is stepwise

options.text: E2 is restricted to tertiary substrates, while E1 is restricted to methyl substrates
options.misconception: believes substrate preference runs opposite to the mechanism reality

options.text: The two differ only in temperature, since the strength of the base never matters
options.misconception: believes base strength has no bearing on which pathway runs

questions.explanation: E2 is concerted: the base removes a beta hydrogen in the same step that the double bond forms and the leaving group departs, so a strong base is needed and the substitution is stereospecific. E1 is stepwise: the leaving group ionises first to give a carbocation, so a weak base suffices and rearrangements become possible. Sterically hindered tertiary substrates block the concerted approach and so favour E1.
questions.hint: Ask whether the leaving group departs before or in the same step as the hydrogen is removed.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state what Markovnikov's rule predicts
questions.stem: A hydrogen halide adds across the double bond of an unsymmetrical alkene with no peroxide present. What does Markovnikov's rule say happens?

options.text: The hydrogen goes to the carbon that already carries the larger number of hydrogens
The hydrogen goes to the carbon that carries the smaller number of hydrogens
options.misconception: applies the anti-Markovnikov outcome to a reaction with no peroxide

options.text: The hydrogen and the halogen both end up on the same carbon of the double bond
options.misconception: believes a new bond forms between the two incoming fragments

options.text: The halogen goes to the more substituted carbon and the hydrogen to the less substituted one
options.misconception: reverses both assignments of the Markovnikov product

questions.explanation: The proton adds first to the end that gives the more stable carbocation, which is the carbon bearing more hydrogens, because that carbon gains a hydrogen and stays the more substituted site. The halide then lands on the carbocation centre. This is what happens with no peroxide present; the opposite regiochemistry needs a radical chain, which only hydrogen bromide supports cleanly under peroxide initiation.
questions.hint: Ask where the positive charge would be more stable after the proton adds.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: classify a halogen substituent as activating or deactivating
questions.stem: A halogen is attached directly to a benzene ring, and a later substitution is planned on that same ring. What is true of that halogen substituent?

options.text: Deactivating, but it steers the later substitution to the ortho and para positions
Activating, but it steers the later substitution to the meta position
options.misconception: pairs deactivating strength with a meta steer, which is not a real combination

options.text: Activating, and it steers the later substitution to the ortho and para positions
options.misconception: believes halogens donate electron density and behave like an alkyl group

options.text: Deactivating, and it steers the later substitution to the meta position
options.misconception: applies the meta steer of a carbonyl substituent to a halogen

questions.explanation: A halogen pulls electron density through the sigma framework, which slows attack and makes it deactivating, but it also donates a lone pair into the ring by resonance, and that donation is strongest at the ortho and para carbons. Because the resonance effect controls where the new group lands, halogens are the classic case of a substituent that is deactivating and yet ortho and para directing, which is why halogenated rings still give para products as the major isomer.
questions.hint: Weigh the inductive pull against the lone pair donation separately.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: assign partial charges across a carbonyl group
questions.stem: A carbonyl group consists of a carbon and an oxygen joined by a double bond. Which statement describes its polarity correctly?

options.text: Oxygen draws the shared density, so the carbon is partially positive
Carbon draws the shared density, so the oxygen is partially positive
options.misconception: reverses which of the two atoms is the electronegative partner

options.text: The two atoms share the density evenly, so the group is nonpolar
options.misconception: believes a double bond forces equal sharing of the electron pairs

options.text: The double bond shares a single pair, so the group carries no dipoles at all
options.misconception: believes one shared pair means no bond dipole exists

questions.explanation: Oxygen is markedly more electronegative than carbon, so both shared pairs of the double bond are pulled towards the oxygen, leaving it partially negative and the carbon partially positive. That polarity is the whole reason a carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles rather than by electrophiles, and it is why aldehydes and ketones react readily with nucleophiles at that carbon.
questions.hint: Compare the electronegativities of the two atoms in the bond.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone
questions.stem: An aldehyde and a ketone hold the same total number of carbon atoms. Which statement states the difference between the two classes?

options.text: An aldehyde carries at least one hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon
An aldehyde carries no oxygen anywhere in its functional group
options.misconception: believes the aldehyde functional group contains no oxygen at all

options.text: An aldehyde is in fact a primary alcohol written in another form
options.misconception: confuses a carbonyl class with the alcohol functional group

options.text: A ketone carries at least one hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon
options.misconception: reverses the definition, assigning the carbonyl hydrogen to the ketone

questions.explanation: Both classes contain the carbonyl group, so the oxygen is present in each, and the split is made by what is attached to the carbonyl carbon. An aldehyde has at least one hydrogen there, which is why it is the more reactive of the two and oxidises readily, whereas a ketone has two carbon groups there and resists oxidation. Remembering which end of the definition belongs to which class avoids reversing them.
questions.hint: Look at what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon in each class.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Ester hydrolysis under acid and base
questions.learningObjective: compare acid and base hydrolysis of an ester
questions.stem: An ester is first treated with water and acid, then separately with water and base. Which statement describes the two outcomes correctly?

options.text: The acid route is reversible and yields acid and alcohol, the base route is not reversible and yields the carboxylate salt
Both routes are reversible and both yield the acid and the alcohol
options.misconception: believes the base route also rebuilds the ester

options.text: The base route is reversible and yields the acid, the acid route is not reversible
options.misconception: swaps the reversibility of the two routes

options.text: Neither route hydrolyses the ester, since only a metal will break that bond
options.misconception: believes hydrolysis of an ester requires a metal rather than water

questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis is an ordinary equilibrium, so the carboxylic acid and alcohol that form recondense unless the water is in excess or the products are removed. In base the carboxylic acid is trapped as its carboxylate salt, which has no hydroxyl left to attack the acyl carbon, so the reaction runs to completion and is called saponification. That trapping, not the basicity itself, is what makes the base route irreversible.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the acid product in each medium.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: The pair that makes a buffer
questions.learningObjective: state the composition of a buffer solution
questions.stem: A solution holds its pH steady when a small amount of acid is added and then a small amount of base. Which composition achieves that?

options.text: A weak acid together with a substantial amount of its conjugate base salt
A strong acid together with a strong base present in equal amounts
options.misconception: believes a strong acid and strong base pair can act as a buffer

options.text: A single weak acid with no salt of that acid anywhere in the solution
options.misconception: believes a weak acid alone resists added base and acid alike

options.text: Pure water carrying dissolved gas and no dissolved salt of any kind
options.misconception: believes dissolved gas alone constitutes a buffer system

questions.explanation: Buffering needs both partners of a conjugate pair present in useful amounts, because added base is consumed by the weak acid and added acid is consumed by the conjugate base. A weak acid on its own has no conjugate base to soak up added acid, and a strong acid with strong base neutralises completely rather than absorbing small additions. The ratio between the two partners is what sets the pH, and their concentration sets the capacity.
questions.hint: Ask which partner neutralises an added acid and which neutralises an added base.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Carbon inventory from a gas sample
questions.learningObjective: convert a mass of carbon dioxide into moles of carbon
questions.stem: A 3.30 g sample of carbon dioxide is analysed. How many moles of carbon atoms does that sample contain? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: One mole of carbon dioxide, 44.01 g per mol, holds one mole of carbon atoms, so 3.30 g holds 3.30 divided by 44.01, which is 0.0750 mol. The trap is dividing by 12.01 instead, which gives the mass of carbon alone and overstates the amount by a factor of the oxygen mass.
questions.hint: The mole ratio of carbon dioxide to carbon is one to one, so use the whole molar mass.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Hydrogen inventory from a water sample
questions.learningObjective: convert a mass of water into moles of hydrogen atoms
questions.stem: A 2.70 g sample of water is analysed. How many moles of hydrogen atoms does that sample contain? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: One mole of water, 18.02 g per mol, holds two moles of hydrogen atoms, so 2.70 g holds 2 times 2.70 divided by 18.02, which is 0.300 mol. Reporting 0.150 mol is the common slip, because it counts water molecules rather than hydrogen atoms inside them.
questions.hint: Count the atoms of hydrogen inside each molecule, not the molecules.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: obtain a molecular formula from an empirical formula and a molar mass
questions.stem: A hydrocarbon is 85.6 percent carbon and 14.4 percent hydrogen by mass, which gives the empirical formula CH2, and its molar mass is 56.11 g per mol. What whole number multiplies that empirical formula?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is the molar mass divided by the empirical formula mass, so 56.11 divided by 14.03, which is 4.00. The multiplier must come out as a whole number, and dividing by 12.01 instead of by the formula mass gives 4.67, which cannot scale a formula and shows the calculation is on the wrong quantity.
questions.hint: Divide the molar mass by the mass of the whole empirical formula unit.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: count rings and pi bonds from a molecular formula
questions.stem: A compound has the molecular formula C8H10. How many rings plus pi bonds does a single molecule of it contain? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: For a hydrocarbon the count is two times the carbons plus two minus the hydrogens, all divided by two, which is 16 plus 2 minus 10 over two, so 4. An ethylbenzene or a xylene fits, since each has one ring and three pi bonds, and forgetting the ring would report 3.
questions.hint: Subtract the hydrogens from the fully saturated acyclic formula, then halve.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute a molar mass from a molecular formula
questions.stem: Tetradecane has the formula C14H30. What is its molar mass in grams per mole, using 12.01 for carbon and 1.008 for hydrogen? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The molar mass is 14 times 12.01 plus 30 times 1.008, which is 168.14 plus 30.24, so 198.38 g per mol. Using 12.00 and 1.00 as whole numbers gives 198, which is close but drops the decimals that make the figure agree with the periodic table values.
questions.hint: Multiply each element's count by its atomic mass and add.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: find moles of hydrogen consumed by hydrogenation
questions.stem: Benzene is fully hydrogenated to cyclohexane. How many moles of hydrogen gas are consumed per 0.35 mol of benzene? Report the number only.

Halving that, to 0.525 mol, would count the product carbons rather than the pi bonds that must be saturated.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Mass of a product by addition
questions.learningObjective: find the mass of an addition product
questions.stem: Hydrogenation of 0.250 mol of ethene consumes an equal amount of hydrogen gas. What mass of ethane, in grams, is produced? Use 12.01 for carbon and 1.008 for hydrogen.
questions.explanation: The addition is one to one, so 0.250 mol of ethene gives 0.250 mol of ethane, whose molar mass is 2 times 12.01 plus 6 times 1.008, that is 30.07 g per mol, and 0.250 of that is 7.52 g. Subtracting the mass of the hydrogen taken up instead of adding it would give 7.01 g, which breaks conservation of mass.
questions.hint: Check your answer by adding the masses of the two reactants.

questions.learningObjective: find the mass of an ester from esterification stoichiometry

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute a percent yield for a product isolated
questions.stem: A reaction is expected to give 8.810 g of ethyl ethanoate from 0.100 mol of ethanoic acid, and 6.62 g of solid is isolated. What percent yield was achieved? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Percent yield is the isolated mass divided by the theoretical mass, times 100, so 6.62 over 8.810 is 75.1 percent. Dividing by the mass of the acid used, which would report about 75 percent of a different quantity, is not a yield at all because the acid is not the product.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: count stereoisomers from the number of chiral centres
questions.stem: An open-chain molecule has three chiral centres and no internal symmetry of any kind. How many stereoisomers are possible for it? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With n independent chiral centres and no symmetry to collapse duplicates, the number of stereoisomers is two to the n, so 2 cubed is 8, which is 4 enantiomer pairs. Halving that to 4 would ignore the mirror-image partners, and multiplying beyond 8 would double count configurations that are mirror images of one another.
questions.hint: Each centre doubles the count, and every configuration has a mirror partner.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Monosubstitution products from a branched alkane
questions.learningObjective: count distinct monosubstitution products using symmetry
questions.stem: How many distinct products can be formed by replacing exactly one hydrogen of 2-methylbutane with a chlorine atom? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The molecule has a central carbon bearing a hydrogen, a methylene group, and two methyl groups that are equivalent by symmetry, plus the methyl at the far end. The four kinds of hydrogen are therefore the central one, the two on the methylene, the two equivalent methyls on the branch carbon, and the three on the end methyl, so four products form. Counting the five carbons separately would give five, which wrongly treats the two equivalent methyls as different.
questions.hint: Find the symmetry of the skeleton and merge any equivalent positions.

questions.learningObjective: count the structural isomers of a given alkane formula

questions.explanation: The five are n-hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane, which is every distinct way of joining six carbons in a chain with only single bonds. 3,3-dimethylbutane is not on the list because its longest chain is four carbons, so it is the same compound as 2,2-dimethylbutane written badly.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: count the structural isomers of a smaller alkane formula

questions.learningObjective: explain how glucose forms two anomers in solution
questions.stem: Explain how an aqueous solution of D-glucose produces two different ring forms, and state which feature of the molecule is responsible.

answer.exemplar: The aldehyde group at C1 and a hydroxyl on the same chain react with each other, so the carbonyl oxygen and an OH group join in an intramolecular hemiacetal and a six-membered ring forms. The former carbonyl carbon now carries a new OH, and that carbon is a new stereocentre, because the ring can close with the new OH pointing either way. The two closures give the alpha anomer, with that OH opposite the ring hydroxyl, and the beta anomer, with it on the same side, and the two interconvert in water through the open-chain form.

questions.explanation: The aldehyde group at C1 and a hydroxyl on the same chain react with each other, so the carbonyl oxygen and an OH group join in an intramolecular hemiacetal and a six-membered ring forms. The former carbonyl carbon now carries a new OH, and that carbon is a new stereocentre, because the ring can close with the new OH pointing either way. The two closures give the alpha anomer, with that OH opposite the ring hydroxyl, and the beta anomer, with it on the same side, and the two interconvert in water through the open-chain form.
questions.hint: Follow what happens to the former carbonyl carbon when the ring closes.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: explain how an enzyme speeds a reaction without changing its feasibility
questions.stem: Explain how an enzyme can speed up a reaction while leaving unchanged whether that reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

answer.exemplar: An enzyme binds its reactants and holds them in the arrangement that suits the reaction, which provides a pathway whose transition state sits lower, so the activation energy of that pathway is smaller and more molecules cross it each second. The enzyme does not change the free energy difference between the starting materials and the products, because it does not change the initial and final states, only the route between them. It therefore cannot make an unfavourable reaction favourable, and the equilibrium it eventually reaches is the same one that would be reached without it.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of electrophilic aromatic substitution
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe bromination of benzene with a halogenating catalyst present. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The intermediate loses a proton, and that carbon-hydrogen bond's electrons restore the ring
The catalyst polarises the bromine molecule so that a strongly electrophilic bromine species forms
The hydrogen ion and the bromide ion leave the mixture together as the acid by-product
A ring pi bond attacks the electrophile, giving an intermediate with a positive charge

questions.explanation: The catalyst acts first, making the halogen molecule electrophilic, because no electrophile exists until then. The ring pi bond then attacks that electrophile, and the resulting carbocation intermediate is dearomatised, so the ring is temporarily nonaromatic. Loss of the proton from the carbon that was attacked returns the electrons to the ring and restores aromaticity, and the proton and the halide ion leave together as the acid by-product. Reversing the first two steps is impossible, since there is no electrophile before the catalyst has acted, and reversing the last two would leave a ring that never recovers its aromaticity.
questions.hint: No electrophile exists until the catalyst has acted, and the ring only regains aromaticity at the proton loss.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of base-promoted ester hydrolysis
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe the base-promoted hydrolysis of an ester. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The intermediate collapses and the alkoxide group leaves the acyl carbon
The carboxylate salt and the alcohol now sit in the mixture, so the hydrolysis cannot reverse
A hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon and the double bond opens onto the oxygen
The carboxylic acid and alkoxide that have just formed react, and the alkoxide takes a proton from the acid

questions.explanation: Attack has to come first, because the hydroxide ion is the electron pair that opens the carbonyl pi bond and creates the tetrahedral intermediate. That intermediate then collapses, which pushes the alkoxide out of the molecule and restores the carbonyl on the acyl carbon. The carboxylic acid and the alkoxide that result react with each other, so the alkoxide takes a proton from the acid and the pair becomes a carboxylate and an alcohol. With no carboxylic acid left, the carboxylate cannot attack the acyl carbon, so the reaction is driven to completion and is called saponification.
questions.hint: Collapse cannot precede attack, and the carboxylate salt is the final state.
